subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Energy moves between system and surroundings; the total never changes
Exothermic or endothermic: which way the energy goes
Energy profiles: relative stability decides the direction
Finding ΔH⦵ from a temperature change
Bond breaking costs energy, bond forming releases it
Hess's law: the route does not matter
Incomplete combustion: carbon monoxide and soot
Comparing coal, oil and natural gas
Biofuels: renewable, but not carbon neutral
Fuel cells: chemical energy straight to electricity

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the temperature of a substance?
options: The form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold one
A measure of the total kinetic energy of all the particles it has
A quantity that has to rise whenever heat is transferred into it
A measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles
optionWhy: A student who treats heat and temperature as the same thing picks this. What flows from a hot object to a cold one is heat, energy transferred because of the temperature difference; temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.

A student who thinks temperature depends on the amount of substance picks this. A total would be larger for a larger sample, but a bucket and a cup of water can be at the same temperature. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.

A student who equates being heated with getting hotter picks this. During a change of state, such as boiling, heat is transferred into the substance while its temperature stays constant. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.

Temperature is an average over the particles: it measures how fast, on average, they are moving. It does not depend on how many particles there are, and it is not itself a form of energy that is transferred.
questions.explain: Temperature is an average over the particles: it measures how fast, on average, they are moving. It does not depend on how many particles there are, and it is not itself a form of energy that is transferred.

questions.q: Solid ammonium nitrate is dissolved in water in a polystyrene cup, and the temperature of the water falls from 21.0 °C to 15.5 °C. Which statement explains the fall in temperature?
options: Energy is transferred from the water to the dissolving solid, so the process is endothermic.
The solution is the system; it loses energy, so its temperature falls and the process is exothermic.
Cold is released by the dissolving solid and spreads out through all of the water in the polystyrene cup.
Energy is used up as the solid dissolves, so the total energy of everything decreases.
optionWhy: The dissolving solid is the system and the water is part of the surroundings. The system takes in energy from the water, so the water's temperature falls: the process is endothermic, with a positive ΔH.

A student who treats the solution as the system reads the fall in temperature as the system losing energy. The thermometer measures the water, which is part of the surroundings; the water has lost energy to the system, so the process is endothermic.
A student who thinks of cold as something that can be given out picks this. Only energy is transferred: the water becomes colder because energy passes from it into the dissolving solid.
A student who thinks processes use energy up picks this. Energy is conserved: the energy that leaves the water is taken in by the dissolving solid, so the total energy is unchanged.
questions.explain: The dissolving solid is the system and the water is part of the surroundings. The system takes in energy from the water, so the water's temperature falls: the process is endothermic, with a positive ΔH.

questions.q: The energy profile of an endothermic reaction is sketched with reaction coordinate on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis. Which statement about this profile is correct?
options: The products are more stable than the reactants, as they have more energy.
It shows an energy barrier, which the profile of an exothermic reaction lacks.
The products are at a higher potential energy than the reactants.
The distance along the x-axis shows how long the reaction takes.
optionWhy: A student who thinks more energy means more stable picks this. The products do have more potential energy, which makes them less stable than the reactants: lower potential energy means greater stability.

A student who thinks exothermic reactions need no energy to start picks this. Both profiles show an energy barrier (the activation energy). The difference is where the products end: above the reactants for endothermic, below for exothermic.

In an endothermic reaction the system gains energy from the surroundings, so the products end at a higher potential energy than the reactants. The difference between the two levels is ΔH, which is positive.

A student who reads the x-axis as time picks this. The reaction coordinate shows the progress of the particles from reactants to products; the profile gives no information about how long the reaction takes.
questions.explain: In an endothermic reaction the system gains energy from the surroundings, so the products end at a higher potential energy than the reactants. The difference between the two levels is ΔH, which is positive.

questions.q: An energy profile for a reaction is plotted with reaction coordinate on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis. Relative to the same zero, the reactants are at 150 kJ mol⁻¹, the top of the energy barrier is at 280 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products are at 40 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?
options: −110 kJ mol⁻¹
+110 kJ mol⁻¹
+130 kJ mol⁻¹
−240 kJ mol⁻¹
optionWhy: ΔH = potential energy of products − potential energy of reactants = 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. The products lie below the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.

A student who thinks energy given out is a positive quantity reads the fall of 110 kJ mol⁻¹ correctly but gives it a plus sign. ΔH describes the system, which loses energy, so ΔH = 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹.
A student who confuses ΔH with the barrier height takes 280 − 150 = +130 kJ mol⁻¹. That is the activation energy, Ea. ΔH is products minus reactants: 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹.

A student who counts only the fall from the top of the barrier to the products takes 40 − 280 = −240 kJ mol⁻¹. That ignores the 130 kJ mol⁻¹ taken in to reach the top. The net change is 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: ΔH = potential energy of products − potential energy of reactants = 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. The products lie below the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
questions.working: ΔH = potential energy of products − potential energy of reactants = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ − 150 kJ mol⁻¹ = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. (The barrier height above the reactants, 280 − 150 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹, is the activation energy and does not enter ΔH.)

questions.q: The diagram shows the energy profile of a reaction, with four vertical arrows labelled W, X, Y and Z. Which arrow represents the enthalpy change, ΔH, of the reaction?
options: Arrow W
Arrow X
Arrow Y
Arrow Z
optionWhy: W is the height of the energy barrier above the reactants, the energy that must be supplied to start the reaction. ΔH is not the barrier height; it is the difference between the reactant and product levels, arrow Y.

X is the fall from the top of the barrier to the products. That energy is released only after the energy W was absorbed to reach the peak, so the net energy given out is X − W, which is the drop from reactants to products, arrow Y.

ΔH is the difference in potential energy between the products and the reactants, which is the arrow joining the reactant level to the product level. Here the products are lower, so ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic.

Z is the potential energy of the reactants above the axis. That total is not released, because the products still hold most of it; the zero of the axis is arbitrary. Only the difference between the reactant and product levels, arrow Y, is transferred to the surroundings.
questions.explain: ΔH is the difference in potential energy between the products and the reactants, which is the arrow joining the reactant level to the product level. Here the products are lower, so ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: A spirit burner containing ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is used to heat 150.0 g of water in a copper can. Burning 0.920 g of ethanol raises the temperature of the water from 19.0 °C to 40.5 °C. Use c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and A_r values H 1.01, C 12.01, O 16.00. What value of ΔH for the combustion of ethanol do these results give?
options: −6.75 × 10⁵ kJ mol⁻¹
−6.75 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹
−9.25 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹
−1.35 × 10¹ kJ mol⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who does not convert joules to kilojoules divides 13 480 J by 0.01997 mol and quotes −675 000 as kJ mol⁻¹. Q must be divided by 1000 first: ΔH = −13.48 kJ / 0.01997 mol = −675 kJ mol⁻¹.

Q = mcΔT = 150.0 × 4.18 × 21.5 = 13 480 J = 13.48 kJ. n(C₂H₅OH) = 0.920 / 46.08 = 0.01997 mol. ΔH = −Q/n = −13.48 / 0.01997 = −675 kJ mol⁻¹. (This is far less exothermic than the accepted value, −1367 kJ mol⁻¹, largely because much of the energy is transferred to the air and the can rather than to the water.)
A student who adds 273 to the temperature change uses ΔT = 294.5 K, giving Q = 184.7 kJ and ΔH = −9250 kJ mol⁻¹. A temperature change has the same value in K as in °C: ΔT = 21.5 K.

A student who takes the heat measured as ΔH gives it the negative sign of an exothermic change but does not divide by the amount burned, writing ΔH = −13.5 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH is per mole, so Q must be divided by the amount of ethanol burned, 0.01997 mol, giving −675 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: Q = mcΔT = 150.0 × 4.18 × 21.5 = 13 480 J = 13.48 kJ. n(C₂H₅OH) = 0.920 / 46.08 = 0.01997 mol. ΔH = −Q/n = −13.48 / 0.01997 = −675 kJ mol⁻¹. (This is far less exothermic than the accepted value, −1367 kJ mol⁻¹, largely because much of the energy is transferred to the air and the can rather than to the water.)

questions.q: Which statement about the standard enthalpy change of a reaction, ΔH⦵, is correct?
options: It is the heat transferred at constant pressure with every substance in its standard state.
Its value is the same whether a product such as water forms as a liquid or as a gas.
It is the total heat transferred in an experiment, whatever amount of each reactant is used.
It is positive when heat passes from the system into the surroundings at 100 kPa.
optionWhy: This is the definition: ΔH⦵ is the heat transferred at constant pressure, under standard conditions (100 kPa), with each substance in its standard state, for the amounts in the equation, in kJ mol⁻¹.

A student who thinks physical state does not affect ΔH picks this. For H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O, ΔH⦵ is −286 kJ mol⁻¹ for H₂O(l) but −242 kJ mol⁻¹ for H₂O(g), because condensing steam releases energy. ΔH⦵ applies to the states shown.
A student who equates the heat measured with ΔH picks this. The heat measured depends on how much reacts. ΔH⦵ refers to the amounts in the equation and is quoted per mole, in kJ mol⁻¹.
A student who thinks energy given out is a positive quantity picks this. ΔH describes the system. When heat passes from the system to the surroundings, the system loses energy and ΔH⦵ is negative.
questions.explain: This is the definition: ΔH⦵ is the heat transferred at constant pressure, under standard conditions (100 kPa), with each substance in its standard state, for the amounts in the equation, in kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Methane burns in oxygen: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). The reaction is exothermic. Which statement explains why?
options: Forming the bonds in CO₂ and H₂O releases more energy than breaking the bonds in CH₄ and O₂ absorbs.
Breaking the bonds in CH₄ and O₂ releases the stored energy, which passes to the surroundings.
More bonds are formed in CO₂ and H₂O than are broken in CH₄ and O₂, so energy is released.
The energy is stored in the CH₄; the O₂ only lets it be released and has no part in the change.
optionWhy: Breaking the C–H and O=O bonds absorbs energy; forming the C=O and O–H bonds releases energy. Because the bonds formed are stronger in total, more energy is released than absorbed, and the difference is transferred to the surroundings.

A student who thinks bonds store energy that is released when they break chooses this. Breaking any bond, in CH₄ or in O₂, absorbs energy; the energy released comes from forming the bonds in CO₂ and H₂O.

A student who judges by counting bonds chooses this. In fact 6 bonds are broken (4 C–H, 2 O=O) and 6 are formed (2 C=O, 4 O–H); the reaction is exothermic because the bonds formed are stronger, not more numerous.

A student who sees the fuel as the energy store chooses this. The O=O bonds must be broken too, absorbing energy, and the energy released comes from forming bonds in CO₂ and H₂O, which contain the oxygen atoms.
questions.explain: Breaking the C–H and O=O bonds absorbs energy; forming the C=O and O–H bonds releases energy. Because the bonds formed are stronger in total, more energy is released than absorbed, and the difference is transferred to the surroundings.

questions.q: Why is the C–H bond enthalpy in a table of bond enthalpies described as an average value?
options: It is the mean of repeated measurements made on a single compound, taken to reduce the random error in the data.
The energy to break a C–H bond varies from one compound to another, so a mean over many compounds is given.
Values measured in the solid, liquid and gas are pooled into one mean, as the same C–H bonds are present in all three.
Every C–H bond has the same strength; 'average' only means the single measured value has been rounded.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'average' as in a practical write-up chooses this. The averaging is over the same bond in different compounds, not over repeat trials on one compound.

A C–H bond in methane, ethane or ethanol has a slightly different bond enthalpy because the rest of the molecule affects it. The tabulated value is the mean over many compounds, which is why calculations with it give estimates.

A student who thinks bond enthalpies apply in any state, because the same bonds are present in solid, liquid and gas, chooses this. Bond enthalpies are defined for the gaseous state only; changes of state involve intermolecular forces, which are not included, and the averaging is over different compounds.
A student who thinks each bond type has one fixed strength chooses this. The strength of a C–H bond depends on its molecular environment, so values differ between compounds.
questions.explain: A C–H bond in methane, ethane or ethanol has a slightly different bond enthalpy because the rest of the molecule affects it. The tabulated value is the mean over many compounds, which is why calculations with it give estimates.

questions.q: An exothermic reaction P → Q takes place in a single step. With a catalyst, the same reaction takes place by a different route of three steps with a lower activation energy, and is much faster. Both routes start from the same reactants and give the same products under the same conditions. How does ΔH of the catalysed reaction compare with ΔH of the uncatalysed reaction?
options: It is the same, because ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, not the route.
It is smaller in size, because the catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
It is more negative, because each of the three steps adds its own enthalpy change to the total.
It is more negative, because a faster reaction transfers more energy to the surroundings per mole.
optionWhy: By Hess’s law the enthalpy change is independent of the pathway. The catalysed route has three steps and a lower activation energy, but it starts and ends at the same states, so the ΔH values of its steps sum to the same total.
A student who treats the activation energy as part of ΔH chooses this. A catalyst lowers the energy barrier but leaves the energies of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, unchanged.
A student who thinks more steps means a larger energy change chooses this. The steps’ ΔH values (some may be positive) sum to the same total as the one-step route.
A student who links speed with the amount of energy chooses this. The catalysed reaction releases the same energy per mole, only in a shorter time.
questions.explain: By Hess’s law the enthalpy change is independent of the pathway. The catalysed route has three steps and a lower activation energy, but it starts and ends at the same states, so the ΔH values of its steps sum to the same total.

questions.q: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, undergoes complete combustion in oxygen. What amount of oxygen, O₂, reacts with 1.00 mol of ethanol?
options: 3.00 mol
3.50 mol
6.00 mol
1.50 mol
optionWhy: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). The products contain 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 7 O atoms; ethanol supplies 1 of them, so O₂ supplies 6 O atoms, which is 3 O₂. So 1.00 mol of ethanol reacts with 3.00 mol of O₂.

A student who counts the 7 O atoms in the products (2CO₂ + 3H₂O) but takes them all from O₂, giving 3½O₂, picks this. Ethanol already contains one O atom in its –OH group, so O₂ supplies only 6 O atoms: 3.00 mol.
A student who finds that O₂ must supply 6 O atoms and takes that as 6 mol of O₂ picks this. Oxygen is diatomic: each O₂ molecule supplies two O atoms, so 6 O atoms need 3 O₂, i.e. 3.00 mol.

A student who balances only the carbon, forming 2CO₂ (4 O atoms, 3 of them from O₂), and leaves the hydrogen unoxidized picks this. The hydrogen in ethanol also burns, forming 3H₂O, which needs 3 more O atoms: 3.00 mol of O₂ in total.
questions.explain: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). The products contain 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 7 O atoms; ethanol supplies 1 of them, so O₂ supplies 6 O atoms, which is 3 O₂. So 1.00 mol of ethanol reacts with 3.00 mol of O₂.
questions.working: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). O atoms in products = 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 7; O atoms in 1 C₂H₅OH = 1; O atoms from O₂ = 7 − 1 = 6; amount of O₂ = 6/2 = 3 per mol ethanol, so n(O₂) = 3.00 mol.

questions.q: Which equation correctly represents the combustion of an element in excess oxygen?
options: 2Al(s) + O₂(g) → 2AlO(s)
P₄(s) + 5O₂(g) → P₄O₁₀(s)
H₂(g) + O₂(g) → H₂O₂(l)
S(s) + 2O(g) → SO₂(g)
optionWhy: A student who assumes a metal oxide is always one metal to one oxygen, like MgO, picks this. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions and oxide ions are O²⁻, so the formula is Al₂O₃: 4Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Al₂O₃(s).
Phosphorus is a non-metal that burns in excess oxygen to form phosphorus(V) oxide, P₄O₁₀. Every formula is correct (oxygen as O₂) and the equation is balanced: 4 P and 10 O atoms on each side.

A student who balances the oxygen atoms by changing the product's formula to H₂O₂, which is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance, picks this. Hydrogen burns to form water; balance with coefficients: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l).
A student who writes oxygen as single O atoms picks this. Oxygen gas consists of O₂ molecules, so sulfur burns as S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g).
questions.explain: Phosphorus is a non-metal that burns in excess oxygen to form phosphorus(V) oxide, P₄O₁₀. Every formula is correct (oxygen as O₂) and the equation is balanced: 4 P and 10 O atoms on each side.

questions.q: Which equation represents an incomplete combustion of ethanol?
options: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)
C₂H₅OH(l) + 1½O₂(g) → 2C(s) + 3H₂O(l)
C₂H₅OH(l) + 4O(g) → 2CO(g) + 3H₂O(l)
C₂H₅OH(l) + O₂(g) → 2C(s) + 3H₂O(l)
optionWhy: This is the equation for complete combustion. You may think 'incomplete' simply means that some of the fuel is left unburnt, with the same products. Incomplete combustion is defined by its products: carbon (soot) or carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide.

A student who chooses the right products but takes all 3 of their O atoms from O₂ picks this. Ethanol already contains one O atom, so O₂ supplies only 2 O atoms: C₂H₅OH(l) + O₂(g) → 2C(s) + 3H₂O(l). As written, this equation has 4 O atoms on the left and 3 on the right.
Carbon monoxide is a correct product of incomplete combustion, but you wrote oxygen as single O atoms. Oxygen reacts as O₂ molecules: C₂H₅OH(l) + 2O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 3H₂O(l).

In a very limited supply of oxygen the carbon of ethanol is deposited as carbon (soot), while the hydrogen still forms water. The equation is balanced: the products contain 3 O atoms, 1 from ethanol and 2 from O₂.
questions.explain: In a very limited supply of oxygen the carbon of ethanol is deposited as carbon (soot), while the hydrogen still forms water. The equation is balanced: the products contain 3 O atoms, 1 from ethanol and 2 from O₂.

questions.q: Coal has a greater tendency than natural gas to undergo incomplete combustion. Which statement gives a reason for this?
options: Coal contains impurities, and these, not its carbon, form the soot and carbon monoxide.
Coal needs more oxygen per gram than methane, as only the carbon in a fuel uses up oxygen.
Methane is a clean fuel, so its carbon cannot form carbon monoxide or soot.
Coal is a solid, so oxygen reaches only its surface, whereas gas mixes fully with air.
optionWhy: A student who attributes soot to impurities in the coal picks this. Soot is carbon and carbon monoxide contains carbon; both come from the fuel's own carbon when oxygen is limited. Impurities such as sulfur form other pollutants, such as SO₂.

A student who counts only the carbon as needing oxygen picks this. Hydrogen is oxidized to water too, so methane needs more oxygen per gram: 4.0 g of O₂ per gram of CH₄ compared with 2.7 g per gram of carbon. Coal burns incompletely because it is a solid that mixes poorly with air.

A student who treats natural gas as a fuel with no carbon emissions picks this. Methane contains carbon and forms CO or soot whenever its oxygen supply is limited, for example in a Bunsen flame with the air hole closed; it is simply less prone to this than coal.

A gaseous fuel such as methane can mix thoroughly with air before it burns, so every molecule has oxygen nearby. Solid coal, which is mostly carbon, reacts only where oxygen reaches its surface, so the oxygen supply to the carbon is easily limited and CO and soot form.
questions.explain: A gaseous fuel such as methane can mix thoroughly with air before it burns, so every molecule has oxygen nearby. Solid coal, which is mostly carbon, reacts only where oxygen reaches its surface, so the oxygen supply to the carbon is easily limited and CO and soot form.

questions.q: Burning fossil fuels increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. How does this increase lead to warming of the Earth's surface?
options: CO₂ absorbs visible and ultraviolet light coming from the Sun, heating the air.
CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the surface and re-emits some of it back.
CO₂ destroys the ozone layer, so more of the Sun's radiation reaches the surface.
CO₂ forms a layer high in the atmosphere that reflects the surface's heat back down.
optionWhy: A student who places the absorption on the incoming sunlight picks this. CO₂ absorbs little visible or ultraviolet radiation; most sunlight passes through it. CO₂ absorbs the infrared radiation emitted by the warmed surface.

Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface, which emits infrared radiation. CO₂ molecules absorb this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back towards the surface, so more CO₂ means a warmer surface (the enhanced greenhouse effect).

A student who merges the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion picks this. CO₂ does not destroy ozone; ozone depletion (caused mainly by CFCs) concerns ultraviolet radiation. CO₂ warms the surface by absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation.
A student who pictures CO₂ as a mirror-like layer picks this. CO₂ is mixed throughout the atmosphere, and its molecules absorb infrared radiation and re-emit it; they do not reflect it.
questions.explain: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface, which emits infrared radiation. CO₂ molecules absorb this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back towards the surface, so more CO₂ means a warmer surface (the enhanced greenhouse effect).

questions.q: Biofuels are renewable energy sources, whereas fossil fuels are non-renewable. Which statement gives the defining feature of a renewable energy source?
options: It can be collected and used again after it has released its energy.
It adds no carbon dioxide to the atmosphere overall when used.
It comes from a natural source, such as the remains of plants or animals.
It is replenished naturally at least as fast as it is used.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'renewable' as 'reusable' or 'recyclable' picks this. The chemical energy of a fuel is released once, when it burns. Renewable means replenished by natural processes at least as fast as it is used.

A student who links 'renewable' to zero net emissions picks this. Renewable biofuels still add CO₂ overall, from the fossil fuels used to produce them, and a low-carbon source can be non-renewable. The definition concerns the rate of replenishment.

A student who takes natural or biological origin as the test picks this. Coal, oil and natural gas also come from the remains of organisms, but they are non-renewable because they formed over millions of years.
Renewable is about the rate of replacement: new crops for biofuels grow within months or years, whereas coal, oil and gas took millions of years to form and are used far faster than they form.
questions.explain: Renewable is about the rate of replacement: new crops for biofuels grow within months or years, whereas coal, oil and gas took millions of years to form and are used far faster than they form.

questions.q: Plants such as sugar cane, grown to make bioethanol, carry out photosynthesis. Which statement gives the reactants and products of photosynthesis?
options: Glucose reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
Water and soil minerals react to form glucose and oxygen.
Carbon dioxide and water react to form glucose and oxygen gas.
Carbon dioxide reacts to form carbon and oxygen gas.
optionWhy: This is aerobic respiration, the overall reverse of photosynthesis; you interchanged the two processes. In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the reactants and glucose and oxygen are the products.

A student who places the plant's carbon in the soil picks this. Soil minerals supply elements such as nitrogen, not carbon; the carbon in glucose comes from CO₂ in the air, which reacts with water to form glucose and oxygen.

Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g). The carbon in glucose, and so in a biofuel made from it, comes from atmospheric CO₂.

A student who pictures photosynthesis as splitting CO₂, with the plant keeping the carbon, picks this. The carbon becomes part of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, whose hydrogen comes from water, a reactant. The products are glucose and oxygen.
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g). The carbon in glucose, and so in a biofuel made from it, comes from atmospheric CO₂.

questions.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, hydrogen gas is supplied to the anode. Which half-equation represents the reaction at the anode?
options: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
H₂ + 2e⁻ → 2H⁻
optionWhy: Oxidation takes place at the anode: each hydrogen molecule loses two electrons, forming two H⁺ ions that move through the acidic electrolyte to the cathode. The electrons flow through the external circuit.
This is a reduction, the reverse of the anode reaction. You placed reduction at the anode; reduction occurs at the cathode, and at the anode the fuel is oxidized: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻.

A student who applies 'non-metals gain electrons' to hydrogen picks this. In the fuel cell hydrogen is the fuel and is oxidized: it loses electrons and forms H⁺ ions, which the acidic electrolyte carries.
The process is right but hydrogen is written as atoms. Hydrogen gas consists of H₂ molecules, so the half-equation is H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻.
questions.explain: Oxidation takes place at the anode: each hydrogen molecule loses two electrons, forming two H⁺ ions that move through the acidic electrolyte to the cathode. The electrons flow through the external circuit.

questions.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which equation represents the reaction that occurs at the cathode?
options: 4H₂O(l) → 2O₂(g) + 8H⁺(aq) + 8e⁻
O(g) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂O(l)
H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) + heat
O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l)
optionWhy: This is an oxidation (electrons are lost and oxygen gas is formed), the reverse of the cathode reaction. You placed oxidation at the cathode. Oxidation occurs at the anode, where hydrogen is oxidized; at the cathode oxygen is reduced: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
The process is right, but oxygen is written as single atoms. Oxygen gas consists of O₂ molecules, so the half-equation is O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l).

This is the equation for burning hydrogen. You pictured the cell as burning its fuel and using the heat. In a fuel cell hydrogen and oxygen react at separate electrodes and no heat-to-electricity step is involved; at the cathode oxygen is reduced: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
Reduction takes place at the cathode: each O₂ molecule gains four electrons and, with four H⁺ ions from the acidic electrolyte, forms two water molecules. O, H and charge all balance.
questions.explain: Reduction takes place at the cathode: each O₂ molecule gains four electrons and, with four H⁺ ions from the acidic electrolyte, forms two water molecules. O, H and charge all balance.
